title: Jeremiah 22:10–19
context: The prophetic word turns to particular kings, sons of Josiah. The people are told not to weep for the dead, commonly understood as Josiah, who died at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29–30), but to weep for the one who goes away and will not return. The LORD names him Shallum son of Josiah, who reigned in his father’s place and was taken away to die in captivity. Shallum is commonly identified with Jehoahaz, whom Pharaoh Necoh took to Egypt (2 Kings 23:30–34; 2 Chronicles 36:1–4); 1 Chronicles 3:15 lists a Shallum among Josiah’s sons, and the identification, though widely held, rests on comparing these accounts. The LORD then pronounces woe on a king who builds a spacious cedar palace by injustice and unpaid labor, contrasts him with his father, who did justice and righteousness and judged the cause of the poor and needy, and asks, Wasn’t this to know me? The LORD names this king as Jehoiakim son of Josiah and says no one will lament him and he will be buried with the burial of a donkey, dragged and thrown outside Jerusalem’s gates (compare 36:30). 2 Kings 24:6 says only that Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and 2 Chronicles 36:6 speaks of Nebuchadnezzar binding him; interpreters discuss how these accounts relate without forcing them together. Arminian and Reformed readers generally keep these oracles in their historical frame and share the conviction that knowing God shows itself in justice for the poor.

verses.text: Don’t weep for the dead. Don’t bemoan him; but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he will return no more, and not see his native country.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the call not to weep for the dead, commonly taken as Josiah, but for the one who goes away and will not return. Exile is a deeper grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lament redirected from the fallen king to the exiled son. Both traditions commonly read the verse within the history of Josiah’s sons (compare 2 Kings 23:29–34).

verses.text: For the LORD says touching Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went out of this place: “He won’t return there any more.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD speaking of Shallum son of Josiah, who reigned after his father and went out never to return. He is commonly identified with Jehoahaz.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the identification with Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:30–34) as widely held, though based on comparing accounts. Readers in both traditions commonly hold it with appropriate care.

verses.text: But he will die in the place where they have led him captive. He will see this land no more.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying Shallum will die in the place of his captivity and never see the land again. His exile is permanent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word fulfilled in the account of Jehoahaz taken to Egypt (compare 2 Kings 23:34). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober statement of a king’s end.

verses.text: “Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his rooms by injustice; who uses his neighbor’s service without wages, and doesn’t give him his hire;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD pronouncing woe on one who builds his house by injustice and does not pay his workers. Exploitation is condemned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the law’s demand to pay wages promptly (compare Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:15). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about justice for laborers.

verses.text: who says, ‘I will build myself a wide house and spacious rooms,’ and cuts out windows for himself, with a cedar ceiling, and painted with red.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king planning a wide house with spacious rooms, windows, cedar, and red paint. Luxury is pursued at others’ expense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see self-glorifying ambition in the king’s building. Both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical frame as a portrait of royal excess (compare Isaiah 5:8).

verses.text: “Should you reign because you strive to excel in cedar? Didn’t your father eat and drink, and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether competing in cedar makes one a king, and pointing to his father, who did justice and righteousness. True kingship is shown in justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast between the son’s luxury and Josiah’s righteousness (compare 2 Kings 23:25). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to just rule.

verses.text: He judged the cause of the poor and needy; so then it was well. Wasn’t this to know me?” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying that Josiah judged the cause of the poor and needy, and asking, Wasn’t this to know me? Knowing God is shown in how one treats the vulnerable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see knowledge of God expressed in justice (compare Jeremiah 9:24; Hosea 6:6). Both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground: true knowledge of God bears fruit in care for the poor (compare 1 John 3:17).

verses.text: But your eyes and your heart are only for your covetousness, for shedding innocent blood, for oppression, and for doing violence.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying the king’s eyes and heart are set on covetousness, innocent blood, oppression, and violence. His priorities are corrupt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s heart exposed (compare Jeremiah 26:23; 2 Kings 24:4). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober indictment in its historical setting.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: “They won’t lament for him, saying, ‘Ah my brother!’ or, ‘Ah sister!’ They won’t lament for him, saying ‘Ah lord!’ or, ‘Ah his glory!’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD naming Jehoiakim son of Josiah and saying no one will lament him as brother, sister, lord, or glory. His death will bring no mourning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the absence of lament as a mark of judgment on an unjust king. Both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical frame, without speculating beyond the text.

verses.text: He will be buried with the burial of a donkey, drawn and cast out beyond the gates of Jerusalem.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying Jehoiakim will be buried like a donkey, dragged outside the gates. Interpreters commonly compare 36:30 and 2 Kings 24:6 without forcing them together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a humiliating end announced for the king. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse alongside 2 Kings 24:6 and 2 Chronicles 36:6, holding questions about the details with care.
